readerTitle: Why 15% growth beats 10% by far more than 5 points
caseNote: 가상 사례 (포장재 제조사, 구독형 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 복리 계산과 72의 법칙은 표준 재무 개념
insight: 성장률의 작은 차이는 시간이 지나면 결과의 큰 차이가 된다. 같은 크기의 일회성 효과보다 매번 쌓이는 개선을 먼저 본다.
misconception: 성장률이 1.5배 높으면 20년 뒤 결과도 1.5배 정도 크다. 한 번에 크게 얻는 것이 작은 개선을 꾸준히 쌓는 것보다 낫다.

cards.title: Two factories, one small difference
body: Two packaging makers each have $10 million in sales. One grows 10% a year. The other grows 15%.
Five points apart. It sounds like a modest gap. Twenty years later, it is anything but modest.

image.label: Two factories, one growing much taller over time
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 나란히 선 두 공장 건물. 왼쪽은 층이 조금씩, 오른쪽은 층이 점점 더 빠르게 쌓여 훨씬 높아짐. 굴뚝 대신 위로 뻗는 화살표. 실제 기업 로고 없음.

cards.title: How much bigger is the faster factory after 20 years?
body: Both start at $10 million. One grows 10% every year, the other 15%. Neither slows down.
After 20 years, how much larger is the 15% company?

options.text: About 1.5 times larger, since 15 is 1.5 times 10
options.feedback: It feels fair, but it treats growth like a fixed amount added each year. Each year's growth is earned on a bigger base.
Right. The 10% company reaches about $67 million. The 15% company reaches about $164 million. The next card shows how.
Good instinct that the gap widens a lot. Over 20 years it comes to about 2.4 times. Stretch it to 40 years and it passes 5.

cards.title: The gap starts small, then runs away.
body: Sales in millions of dollars. At year 5 the two are only $4 million apart. By year 20 the gap is nearly $100 million.

cards.title: Compound growth
body: **Compound growth** means each period's growth is added to the base, so the next period grows from a bigger number. Growth earns growth.

A quick check is the *rule of 72*: divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years it takes to double. At 10%, about 7 years. At 15%, under 5. The faster company doubles more often, and every doubling is bigger than the last.

image.label: Doubling steps at 10% and 15% on a timeline
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 두 줄. 위 줄(10%)은 약 7년마다, 아래 줄(15%)은 약 5년마다 블록이 두 배로 커짐. 가운데에 "72 ÷ rate = years to double" 문구.

cards.title: Short periods hide the effect, and it cuts both ways.
body: A software company growing 5% a month does not grow 60% a year. It grows about **80%**, because each month builds on the last.
The same math runs in reverse. Lose 3% of subscribers a month and about 31% are gone within a year. Every month you lose a share of a smaller base, but the losses keep stacking up.

cards.title: Anything that feeds on itself compounds.
body: Profits that are put back into the business compound. So do customers who bring in more customers, a team that gets a little faster each quarter, or a factory that cuts scrap by a bit every year.
One-time wins do not. A big order or a single price rise lifts you once, then stops. The useful question is: *does this gain make the next gain easier?*

cards.title: Compounding needs time, and no big losses.
body: Rates rarely hold steady. Growth usually slows as a business gets bigger, so a plan that compounds 15% for 20 years is often a fantasy dressed up as a spreadsheet.
Large losses also break the chain. Fall 50% and you need a 100% gain just to get back to where you started. Steady progress usually beats a fast rate that sometimes collapses.

image.label: A rising curve interrupted by a steep drop
image.brief: 부드럽게 올라가는 복리 곡선이 중간에 절반으로 뚝 떨어진 뒤 다시 원래 높이까지 오래 걸려 올라가는 그래프. "−50% needs +100%" 라벨.

cards.title: Now it's a subscription app.
body: Your app has 10,000 paying subscribers. Each month 4% cancel. You have budget for one project this quarter.

options.text: A promotion that adds 1,500 subscribers right away
options.feedback: It looks best at first and leads by about 100 subscribers after a year. But those new subscribers leak at 4% too, and by year two you are about 500 behind option B.

options.text: Fix onboarding so monthly cancellations fall from 4% to 3%
options.feedback: A small change in a rate that repeats every month. It starts slower, then pulls ahead and keeps widening the gap for as long as it lasts.

options.text: Run the same promotion again every year
options.feedback: You keep paying for new subscribers while 4% of the base still leaves every month. You are refilling a leaking bucket instead of fixing the leak.

cards.title: Small rates, repeated, beat big one-time wins.
body: Over time, the growth rate matters more than the starting size, and a few points add up to multiples.
**Try it today:** find one number in your business that repeats every month, such as returns, cancellations or repeat orders. Ask what a one-point improvement would be worth after three years.
